title: Celiac Disease: Test Before the Gluten-Free Diet
bottomLine: Celiac disease should be confirmed while the patient is consuming gluten. Use appropriate serology with total IgA/context, proceed to endoscopic biopsy or specialist pathway when indicated, and do not diagnose or exclude celiac disease from symptoms alone or after the patient has already removed gluten without a plan.
recognize: Diarrhea, bloating, iron deficiency, weight loss, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis, infertility and neurologic symptoms can all occur.
First-degree relatives and autoimmune conditions increase pretest probability.
differentiate: IBS/non-celiac gluten sensitivity can mimic symptoms but do not produce the same autoimmune enteropathy.
IgA deficiency can produce a false-negative standard IgA-based serology and requires an alternate testing strategy.
assessment: Ask about current gluten intake, family history, autoimmune disease, anemia/weight change, bone disease, pregnancy/fertility and prior testing or self-directed diet changes.
workup: Use tissue-transglutaminase IgA with total IgA in most patients while consuming gluten; use appropriate IgG-based testing when IgA deficient.
Refer for endoscopy/biopsy or specialist assessment when serology/clinical context warrants it; avoid indiscriminate food-allergy testing.
management: Use a strict lifelong gluten-free diet after diagnosis with dietitian support and correction of nutritional deficiencies.
Persistent symptoms require review of adherence, inadvertent gluten exposure, alternate diagnosis and refractory disease rather than simply intensifying dietary restriction.
medicationSafety: Review iron, folate, B12, vitamin D/calcium and other deficiencies individually rather than giving broad supplements indefinitely.
Check excipients only when clinically relevant; do not create unnecessary medication avoidance from unverified gluten concerns.
counselling: Explain why testing must occur before starting a gluten-free diet and why cross-contamination matters after diagnosis.
followUp: Track symptoms, serologic response when appropriate, nutritional status and bone/associated autoimmune issues.
examTrap: Telling a patient to start a gluten-free diet before serologic/diagnostic testing, making later confirmation difficult.
oneLinePearl: For celiac disease, diagnose on gluten and treat off gluten.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology clinical practice resources

title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease: Stage Severity, Withdrawal Risk, and Ongoing Alcohol Harm
bottomLine: Alcohol-associated liver disease spans steatosis, hepatitis, fibrosis/cirrhosis and decompensation. Assess current alcohol exposure and withdrawal risk nonjudgmentally, stage liver severity and complications, treat alcohol-use disorder alongside liver disease, and escalate jaundice/coagulopathy/encephalopathy/infection or GI bleeding urgently.
recognize: Alcohol history may be under-reported because of stigma; biomarkers cannot replace a respectful exposure history.
Alcohol-associated hepatitis can present with jaundice, systemic inflammation and liver dysfunction in a person with heavy ongoing/recent alcohol exposure.
differentiate: AST/ALT pattern can support but does not prove alcohol causation; viral, metabolic, autoimmune, medication/toxin and ischemic causes must still be considered.
Alcohol withdrawal and hepatic encephalopathy can both cause altered mental status but require different management.
assessment: Assess quantity/frequency, last drink, prior withdrawal/seizures, nutrition, medications, jaundice, ascites, bleeding, infection, encephalopathy, other substance use and psychosocial supports.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal function, liver chemistry, bilirubin/INR/albumin and cause-directed testing; assess fibrosis/cirrhosis using validated noninvasive/specialty pathways.
Evaluate infection and GI bleeding promptly when decompensated disease is present.
management: Treat withdrawal safely, support nutrition including thiamine when indicated, manage cirrhosis complications and engage addiction treatment/medications appropriate to liver function.
Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis or decompensation requires hepatology/hospital assessment rather than outpatient abstinence advice alone.
medicationSafety: Sedatives can worsen respiratory/CNS status and must be selected carefully in liver disease/withdrawal.
AUD pharmacotherapy requires liver/renal and interaction review; do not assume every AUD medication is safe in advanced liver disease.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language, discuss abstinence as the most important disease-modifying intervention for alcohol-related liver injury, and offer active treatment for AUD rather than advice alone.
followUp: Track alcohol treatment engagement, liver severity/complications, nutrition and hepatocellular carcinoma/variceal surveillance when cirrhosis is present.
examTrap: Attributing all abnormal liver tests to alcohol and failing to assess withdrawal risk or another concurrent cause of liver injury.
oneLinePearl: Treat the liver disease and the alcohol-use disorder together.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver resources
Canadian alcohol-use-disorder and hepatology practice principles

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Diagnose Clinically and Find the Precipitant
bottomLine: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical syndrome in the setting of significant liver dysfunction/portosystemic shunting. Look for and treat precipitants, use evidence-based ammonia-lowering therapy, and do not diagnose, stage or follow HE from serum ammonia levels alone.
recognize: Altered attention, sleep reversal, disorientation, asterixis and reduced consciousness can occur.
Common precipitants include infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration/overdiuresis, electrolyte/renal disturbance and sedating medications.
differentiate: Delirium from sepsis, intracranial disease, intoxication/withdrawal, hypoglycemia and medication toxicity can coexist or mimic HE.
A high ammonia level without compatible clinical syndrome does not establish HE; a normal/low result should trigger diagnostic reconsideration but does not replace clinical assessment.
assessment: Assess airway/GCS, infection, bleeding, stool/constipation, volume status, renal/electrolytes, medications/sedatives, alcohol withdrawal, focal neurologic signs and baseline cognition.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal/liver tests, glucose, infection/GI-bleed evaluation and neuroimaging only when the differential warrants it.
Do not order serial ammonia to titrate treatment response.
management: Treat the precipitating cause and use lactulose titrated to clinical response/stool goal; add rifaximin for recurrence/appropriate specialist-guided indications.
Protect airway and escalate severe encephalopathy or diagnostic uncertainty to acute care.
medicationSafety: Avoid or minimize benzodiazepines, opioids and other CNS depressants when possible.
Overaggressive lactulose causing dehydration/electrolyte loss can itself worsen encephalopathy.
counselling: Teach patients/caregivers early cognitive/sleep changes, bowel-plan adherence and when to seek care.
followUp: After recovery, reconcile precipitating medications, bowel regimen, recurrent-HE prevention and transplant/hepatology care when appropriate.
examTrap: Repeating serum ammonia to decide whether a clinically improving patient is ready for discharge.
oneLinePearl: HE is diagnosed at the bedside; ammonia does not replace the patient.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver practice resources

title: Colorectal Polyps: Surveillance Follows Pathology, Number, Size, and Quality
bottomLine: Post-polypectomy surveillance is determined by the number, size, histology, dysplasia, completeness of removal and quality of the baseline colonoscopy—not by a universal 'repeat in five years' rule. Use the current provincial/specialty surveillance pathway and ensure pathology is actually reviewed.
recognize: Advanced adenomatous features, numerous adenomas, large serrated lesions, piecemeal resection or poor bowel preparation shorten surveillance.
A normal high-quality colonoscopy or low-risk finding may support a longer interval and avoids unnecessary repeat procedures.
differentiate: Screening intervals and post-polypectomy surveillance intervals are not the same.
New alarm symptoms are managed diagnostically rather than waiting for the scheduled surveillance colonoscopy.
assessment: Review exact pathology, number/size/location, resection completeness, bowel preparation, family/hereditary risk and prior colonoscopies.
workup: No new laboratory test substitutes for reviewing the pathology/endoscopy report; obtain missing records before assigning the interval.
Refer possible hereditary polyposis patterns for genetics/GI assessment.
management: Set the next colonoscopy according to current validated surveillance recommendations and document the reason.
Short-interval site reassessment may be needed after large piecemeal resection or uncertain completeness.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural anticoagulant/antiplatelet plans depend on thrombotic risk and planned intervention; do not apply a universal stop interval.
redFlags: New GI bleeding/iron-deficiency anemia or weight loss before scheduled surveillance
counselling: Explain why surveillance timing is individualized and why earlier is not automatically safer.
followUp: Track pathology, referral and recall until the surveillance plan is closed-loop.
examTrap: Assigning the same colonoscopy interval to a small low-risk adenoma and a large piecemeal advanced lesion.
oneLinePearl: Polyp surveillance is a pathology-and-quality decision, not a fixed calendar interval.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology colorectal screening/surveillance resources

title: Dysphagia: Oropharyngeal or Esophageal, Mechanical or Motility?
bottomLine: The first dysphagia decision is localization: difficulty initiating a swallow/coughing suggests oropharyngeal dysfunction; food sticking after swallowing suggests esophageal disease. Progressive solids-to-liquids dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or complete obstruction requires urgent endoscopic evaluation.
recognize: Oropharyngeal dysphagia can cause coughing/choking, wet voice, nasal regurgitation and aspiration.
Mechanical esophageal obstruction often begins with solids; motility disorders can affect solids and liquids.
differentiate: Globus without true swallow impairment is different from dysphagia.
GERD symptoms do not exclude malignancy, eosinophilic esophagitis or stricture when alarm features are present.
assessment: Ask location/sensation, initiation difficulty, solids vs liquids, progression, food impaction, weight loss, reflux, atopy, neurologic disease and aspiration/pneumonia.
workup: Use swallowing assessment/modified barium studies for suspected oropharyngeal dysfunction and upper endoscopy for persistent esophageal dysphagia/alarm features.
Manometry follows when motility disorder is suspected after structural disease is appropriately evaluated.
management: Treat the cause; arrange speech-language/swallow safety measures for oropharyngeal disease and endoscopic/specialty management for structural esophageal disease.
Complete food-bolus obstruction or inability to handle secretions is an emergency.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric pill-swallowing strategies in a patient with unsafe aspiration risk.
Review medications causing esophagitis or dysmotility when clinically relevant.
counselling: Teach texture/swallow strategies only after the swallowing mechanism is assessed; provide emergency advice for food impaction.
followUp: Ensure pathology/endoscopy/manometry or swallow recommendations are tracked to diagnosis and symptom resolution.
examTrap: Treating progressive solid-food dysphagia with an empiric PPI for months without endoscopic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Localize dysphagia first; then decide structure, motility, or swallow safety.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Esophageal Dysphagia guideline

title: Anorectal Symptoms: Do Not Call Every Bleed a Hemorrhoid
bottomLine: Hemorrhoids are common but should not be used to explain rectal bleeding without considering fissure, abscess/fistula, IBD and colorectal malignancy. Use symptom pattern and anorectal exam when appropriate, treat constipation/straining, and escalate pain, systemic illness or unexplained bleeding.
recognize: Internal hemorrhoids commonly cause painless bright-red bleeding/prolapse; fissures often cause sharp pain with defecation; perianal abscess causes focal severe pain/swelling and may cause fever.
differentiate: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid differs from abscess and from routine internal hemorrhoids.
A visible hemorrhoid does not exclude a proximal bleeding source in an older/high-risk patient.
assessment: Ask bleeding amount/pattern, pain, bowel habit, straining, weight loss, anemia symptoms, pregnancy, anticoagulants and colorectal screening history.
workup: Perform inspection/digital/anoscopic assessment when appropriate; use colon evaluation according to age/risk/alarm features rather than assuming a local source.
Systemic illness/severe pain may require urgent imaging/surgical assessment for deep infection.
management: Increase fibre/fluids and reduce straining for uncomplicated hemorrhoids; use topical/symptom therapy selectively.
Persistent bleeding/prolapse, thrombosis or refractory symptoms may require office/surgical intervention; abscess requires drainage, not hemorrhoid cream.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical steroid/anesthetic use without reassessment.
Anticoagulation management for procedures is individualized to bleeding/thrombotic risk.
counselling: Explain bowel-habit prevention and which bleeding/pain changes require diagnostic reassessment.
followUp: Confirm unexplained rectal bleeding is resolved or diagnostically evaluated rather than repeatedly attributing it to known hemorrhoids.
examTrap: Assuming painless rectal bleeding is hemorrhoidal solely because hemorrhoids are visible on exam.
oneLinePearl: A hemorrhoid can bleed, but it does not prove that it is the only bleeding source.

title: GI Tumour Markers: Monitor Selected Cancers, Do Not Screen the Well Patient
bottomLine: CEA, CA 19-9, AFP and other tumour markers are not stand-alone cancer screening tests in asymptomatic average-risk patients. Use them only in the validated disease context—for risk stratification, treatment response or surveillance—and interpret trends with imaging/pathology because benign disease can elevate them and some cancers do not produce them.
recognize: CEA can be elevated by smoking/inflammation and is mainly useful in selected colorectal-cancer follow-up contexts.
CA 19-9 can rise with biliary obstruction/cholangitis and is not a diagnostic test for pancreatic cancer by itself.
differentiate: AFP can support HCC surveillance/diagnostic pathways in selected high-risk liver populations but does not replace imaging.
A normal tumour marker does not exclude malignancy.
assessment: Clarify why the test was ordered, the known cancer/pathology, baseline level, treatment timing, smoking/inflammation/obstruction and current symptoms.
workup: Use tumour markers only as part of the cancer-specific pathway and correlate with imaging/endoscopy/pathology.
Do not order broad tumour-marker panels for unexplained weight loss instead of doing a targeted diagnostic evaluation.
management: Escalate a clinically meaningful rising marker within the appropriate surveillance pathway but confirm with disease-specific assessment before changing therapy.
Resolve reversible confounders such as biliary obstruction when appropriate before overinterpreting the marker.
medicationSafety: Avoid initiating cancer therapy from a tumour marker alone without diagnostic confirmation.
Treatment toxicity monitoring is regimen-specific and separate from tumour-marker response.
redFlags: New GI bleeding/weight loss despite normal marker
counselling: Explain that tumour markers are context tools and are neither universal cancer screens nor perfect recurrence detectors.
followUp: Use the same assay/pathway where possible and track trends only when the result has a defined management role.
examTrap: Ordering CA 19-9 as a screening test for pancreatic cancer in an asymptomatic average-risk adult.
oneLinePearl: Tumour markers help follow selected cancers; they do not diagnose cancer on their own.

title: Chronic Constipation: Alarm Features, Medication Causes, Then Stepwise Treatment
bottomLine: Chronic constipation is usually diagnosed clinically after medication, metabolic and alarm features are reviewed. Start with fibre/fluids/activity when appropriate and evidence-based osmotic/stimulant/secretagogue therapy as needed; use colonoscopy or broad testing only when age/risk/alarm features or refractory symptoms justify it.
recognize: Constipation includes infrequent stool, hard stool, straining, incomplete evacuation or need for manual manoeuvres—not frequency alone.
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium-channel blockers and many other medications commonly contribute.
differentiate: IBS-C includes recurrent abdominal pain related to bowel habit; defecatory disorders may produce excessive straining/incomplete evacuation despite soft stool.
New constipation with weight loss, bleeding or anemia is different from lifelong stable functional constipation.
assessment: Review duration, stool form/frequency, pain/bloating, diet/fluids/activity, medications, neurologic/endocrine disease, pelvic floor symptoms, bleeding/weight loss and screening history.
workup: Use targeted TSH/calcium/CBC or other testing when clinical clues support a secondary cause; avoid routine broad panels/colonoscopy in uncomplicated functional constipation.
Refractory outlet symptoms may require anorectal testing/pelvic-floor referral.
management: Use adequate fibre when appropriate, osmotic laxatives such as PEG, and stepwise additional therapy according to response and patient factors.
Opioid-induced constipation often needs proactive pharmacologic prevention/treatment rather than diet advice alone.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic dependence on ineffective regimens while symptoms worsen; review renal/electrolyte considerations for selected agents.
Pregnancy, frailty and severe renal disease can change treatment choices.
redFlags: New severe constipation in older/high-risk patient
counselling: Teach realistic bowel goals, correct fibre use and that daily stool is not required for health.
followUp: Reassess response and diagnosis; persistent symptoms despite adequate therapy need evaluation for pelvic-floor or structural disease.
examTrap: Ordering colonoscopy solely because a young low-risk patient has chronic constipation with no alarm features.
oneLinePearl: Constipation care starts with causes and alarm features, then uses stepwise therapy—not reflex colonoscopy.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology practice resources
